The time saving is real. No measurable effect reached pay, hours or output.

Stage four is the least intuitive, so it deserves a proper explanation. The clearest evidence is a randomised experiment: seven thousand knowledge workers across sixty-six firms, over six months. Workers who used the tool saved two hours on email each week. That is a measured benefit for each worker. Yet treated and control workers answered the same threads, attended the same meetings and finished the same documents. The authors detected no shift in the quantity or composition of anyone's work.

A second study, on national records rather than software logs, finds the same. It estimates a precise zero on earnings and hours, ruling out effects larger than two per cent two years after ChatGPT's launch. That does not mean nothing happened; it means any effect was too small to tell apart from zero.
